cues.text: In this town, the day you turn eighteen, you get your own robot.
Nobody picks. A crate lands on your doorstep, and whatever is inside is yours for life.
It can be huge. It can be tiny. It can be a hero.
Or it can be a cleaner that loses fights to dust.
My mum got a butler. He has poured her tea every morning for twenty years.
My dad got a foot massager.
That is the whole robot. He says it is the best thing that ever happened to him.
Mum pretends not to hear that.
Then my friends turned eighteen, one by one.
One got a robot so smart it did her homework and then corrected the teacher.
One got a floating hand that follows him around and carries his bag.
And Nora got a shield robot. Nothing gets through it. Not even dodgeballs.
Then it was my turn. My crate was very small.
I opened it. Inside was a head.
Just a head. One robot head, no body, no arms, no instructions.
I shook the crate for the rest of him. Nothing.
Dad said, "Maybe the body is coming on Tuesday." It was not.
I took it to school anyway. That was a mistake.
"Does it talk?" No. "Does it walk?" It is a head.
Somebody asked if I had tried turning it off and on again.
The whole class laughed. Even the floating hand slapped a desk.
I smiled. I went home. I was not smiling at home.
Then one day, at lunch, somebody got picked on.
Brick has a robot he wears: two giant metal arms.
Pip has a robot too. It is a pair of glasses that knows everything.
It knew exactly how much trouble Pip was in.
Brick lifted him up by the backpack, with one finger.
I felt bad for him. So I stood up.
I said, "Put him down."
Brick looked at me. Then he looked at what was in my hands.
I looked too. I was holding a head.
I sat down again.
That night I put the head on my desk and stared at it.
How do you use a head?
I turned it over. I looked in its ears. I looked up its nose.
And there, at the back, under the dust, was one small button.
I pressed it.
The head opened, like a helmet.
So I put it on.
Metal ran down my neck. Over my arms. Down my legs. All the way to my toes.
I was wearing armor. Sleek, silver, head to toe.
It was never a broken robot. It was a suit.
I went to the forest, where nobody could see me fall over.
I held out my hand, and a beam of light cut a tree in half.
Sorry, tree.
Then my feet lit up, and I was flying.
Badly. But flying.
Then I saw somebody below me, between the trees.
An old man, alone, with his legs shaking.
I thought he was lost. I thought he needed help.
So I landed, and I walked over to him.
In half a second, he was not an old man. He was wearing a suit too.
A katana slid out of his arm, and he jumped at me.
My helmet said one word: "Duck."
I ducked. The blade went over my head and into a tree.
He spun around and tried again. And again. And again.
I went backwards so fast I ran out of forest.
So I went up.
He looked up at me. Then his feet lit up too.
He chased me over the trees, and he was a lot better at flying than I was.
I threw a beam of light at him. He cut it in two.
Then he bumped me out of the sky, and down I went.
I landed so hard I made a hole shaped like me.
And that was not all his robot could do.
His other arm folded open into a cannon.
He pointed it at me, and it lit up.
I tried to get up. My suit said, "Rebooting. Please wait."
I could not move. I could not even blink.
What I did not know was that somebody had followed me from school.
Nora. She had watched the whole thing from a bush.
When the cannon lit up, she was already running.
She slid in front of me and threw her shield open.
The blast hit it and went straight up into the sky.
It pushed her back, one step, then two. But nothing got through.
The old man looked at her. He looked at me. And then he was gone.
I said, "Who was that? Why me?"
She said, "That is the one this town threw out."
"He got his robot at eighteen, like everybody. He used it to break things."
"They took it away from him, a long time ago."
Then she looked at my helmet, and she went white.
"No way. That is the same robot as his."
